entities.summary:
Gnaeus Pompeius (Rufus), suffect consul in 31 BC and a scion of the illustrious gens Pompeia, served during the pivotal transitional phase when Octavian, the future Emperor Augustus, was meticulously consolidating his unparalleled authority following the Battle of Actium. Though not a dominant political or military figure in his own right, his appointment to the highest magistracy underscored the nascent principate's strategy of integrating loyal members of the Roman senatorial aristocracy into its new administrative structure, thereby legitimizing the shift from Republic to Empire. His tenure as consul coincided with the critical years immediately preceding Octavian's formal relinquishment of extraordinary powers in 27 BC, a period marked by profound political reorganization across the Roman world.

Pompeius's suffect consulship, which he held from October to December 31 BC alongside Octavian himself, placed him at the heart of Rome's political machinery during a time of immense change. This period saw Octavian begin to dismantle the emergency powers he had accrued during the civil wars, while simultaneously laying the groundwork for his enduring personal rule. As consul, Pompeius would have overseen legislative processes, judicial proceedings, and public administration, all under the direct influence and guidance of the victorious Octavian. His participation symbolized the continuity of traditional Roman governance even as its underlying power dynamics were fundamentally reshaped, allowing Octavian to present his regime as a restoration rather than a revolution.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Gnaeus Pompeius's suffect consulship in 31 BC illustrates Octavian's strategy of incorporating traditional Roman elites into the new imperial order, contributing to the perceived legitimacy and administrative stability of the early Principate. His career highlights the transition from Republic to Empire and the integration of the aristocracy.
